items.t: Prescription cream: same dose for children. Avoid long-term continuous use in infants and children where possible (adrenal suppression can occur even without occlusion). In infants the napkin acts as an occlusive dressing, so limit treatment to a maximum of 7 days if possible.

src.q: In infants and children, long-term continuous topical therapy should be avoided where possible, as adrenal suppression can occur even without occlusion.
In infants, the napkin may act as an occlusive dressing, and increase absorption. Treatment should therefore be limited, if possible, to a maximum of 7 days.

items.t: Skin lesions caused by viral (for example herpes simplex, chickenpox), fungal (for example candidiasis, tinea) or bacterial (for example impetigo) infection.

items.t: Pharmacy-sale cream: untreated bacterial, viral, tuberculous or fungal infection; eyes or face (for example rosacea, perioral dermatitis); ano-genital area; broken or infected skin (impetigo, cold sores, acne, athlete's foot, infected bites and stings); under occlusive dressings or on large areas.

src.q: In the presence of untreated infections of bacterial, viral, tuberculous or fungal origin.

The product should not be used on the eyes or face (for example, in rosacea or perioral dermatoses), the ano-genital area or on broken or infected skin including impetigo, cold sores, acne athlete's foot, or infected bites and stings.
Not for use with an occlusive dressing or on large areas of the body.

items.t: Topical steroid withdrawal: long-term or inappropriate use can cause rebound flares after stopping (intense redness, stinging and burning that can spread beyond the treated area), more likely on the face and flexures. If the condition recurs within days to weeks after successful treatment, suspect withdrawal; re-apply only with caution, with specialist advice, or consider other treatments.

src.q: Long term continuous or inappropriate use of topical steroids can result in the development of rebound flares after stopping treatment (topical steroid withdrawal syndrome).
Reapplication should be with caution and specialist advise is recommended in these cases or other treatment options should be considered.
when prescribing a topical corticosteroid, consider the lowest potency needed

items.t: Infected lesions: use appropriate antimicrobial therapy; if infection spreads, stop the topical corticosteroid and give systemic antimicrobials.

src.q: Appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be used whenever treating inflammatory lesions which have become infected.
Any spread of infection requires withdrawal of topical corticosteroid therapy, and systemic administration of antimicrobial agents.

items.t: Prescription SmPC: prolonged application to the face is undesirable. Pharmacy-sale SmPC: prolonged use is not recommended, because continuous application may cause skin atrophy, striae and superficial vascular dilatation.

src.q: As with all corticosteroids, prolonged application to the face is undesirable.

items.t: SPS: hydrocortisone applied to the skin can be used during breastfeeding (low potency). Avoid infant contact with treated skin; if applied to the breast, wipe off with warm water before feeds. Large areas for long periods may need infant monitoring of feeding, growth and weight.

src.q: When applied to the skin, used rectally or for use in the ear, hydrocortisone can be used during breastfeeding.
This should be removed with warm water before breastfeeding, and be reapplied after feeding.

src.q: Withdrawal reactions - redness of the skin which may extend to areas beyond the initial affected area, burning or stinging sensation, itch, skin peeling, oozing pustules.

items.t: Systemic absorption from skin folds or the nappy area can cause hypercorticism and HPA-axis suppression with prolonged use, more likely in infants and children and under occlusion. MHRA: adrenal suppression (low blood pressure, dizziness, fainting) is life-threatening and needs urgent treatment; stopping suddenly is dangerous.

src.q: Sufficient systemic absorption may also occur in such sites to produce the features of hypercorticism and suppression of the HPA axis after prolonged treatment.
This is a serious, life-threatening condition that needs urgent treatment.
Stopping the topical steroid suddenly is dangerous if there is adrenal suppression
